samples.text:
The diagram shows how ethanol fuel is produced from sugar cane. There are eight stages in this process, from growing sugar cane to deliver the fuel.

Firstly, the sugar cane is grown for 12–18 months. When it is ready, the cane is harvested and cut by a machine. Then it is crushed by rollers and the juice is extracted from it.

The waste from the crushing, which is called bagasse, is fibrous. This waste is burned and it gives the power to the factory, so the factory use its own waste. Meanwhile, yeast is added to the juice and the sugar turns into alcohol, this is fermentation.

After that, in distillation stage, the ethanol is separated from the water. Then the ethanol is mixed with petrol, it is called blending. Finally, the fuel is delivered to the filling stations, where people can buy it.

Overall, the process takes a long time because the sugar cane need more than one year to grow. The main product is ethanol fuel and also the waste bagasse is used to power the factory.
samples.why: Overview placed at the end but relevant · all stages covered with accurate timing · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary with repetition · word form, agreement and comma splice errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates the process by which sugar cane is turned into ethanol, which is then used as a fuel.

Overall, there are eight stages in the process, beginning with the growing of sugar cane and ending with the delivery of fuel to filling stations. A notable feature is that the fibrous waste produced during the process is used to supply energy to the factory itself. The growing stage is the longest, lasting more than a year in some cases.

Initially, sugar cane is grown for between 12 and 18 months before being harvested by machine. The cane is then crushed by rollers in order to extract the juice. The fibrous waste left over, known as bagasse, is not thrown away but is burned to power the factory. This means that the factory makes use of its own waste.

The juice goes through fermentation, during which yeast is added and the sugar is turned into alcohol. This is followed by distillation, where ethanol is separated from water. Next, the ethanol is blended with petrol to produce the final fuel, and in the last stage this fuel is delivered to filling station.
samples.why: Clear overview highlighting the use of waste · logical sequencing with a range of linking expressions · less common vocabulary (bagasse, blended, distillation) · mostly accurate with one minor slip.

samples.text:
The diagram sets out the eight stages involved in converting sugar cane into ethanol fuel.

Broadly, the process moves from agriculture to industrial processing and finally to distribution. One noteworthy aspect is that a by-product is put to use: the fibrous waste generated when the cane is crushed is burned to provide the energy that powers the factory. Only the growing stage is given a duration, and at up to a year and a half it clearly dominates the overall timescale.

The cane is cultivated for a lengthy period of 12–18 months before being harvested mechanically. It is then passed through rollers, which extract the juice, leaving behind the fibrous residue known as bagasse; rather than being discarded, this is burned as fuel for the plant.

The extracted juice subsequently undergoes fermentation, with yeast being added so that the sugar is converted into alcohol. Distillation then separates the ethanol from the water it contains, after which the ethanol is blended with petrol. In the final stage, the finished fuel is transported to filling stations, completing the journey from field to forecourt.
samples.why: Skilful overview framing the process in three phases and noting the by-product · stages sequenced fluently · precise vocabulary (residue, cultivated, forecourt) · wide range of structures · error-free.
